# Global wind belts and ocean currents (trade winds, westerlies, volta do mar, monsoon) (`wind_systems_ocean_currents`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/navigation.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Navigation, transport & exploration (`navigation`)
- Deps: helped by world_geography, ship_design_caravel_carrack, latitude_astrolabe_quadrant
- Core idea: In 1490 Portuguese pilots know the North Atlantic volta do mar. On the return from West Africa they stand offshore and gain latitude until westerlies can carry them towards Portugal. The north-east trades and westward-flowing North Equatorial Current favour a passage from the Canaries towards the Caribbean. For the return, stand north towards the belt of westerlies around the latitude of the Azores before turning east. Columbus demonstrates this circuit in 1492–93. South of the seasonally migrating equatorial convergence zone lie the south-east trades. Southbound ships near southwestern Africa face headwinds and the north-flowing Benguela Current. In 1497 da Gama sails well offshore in the South Atlantic before turning back towards southern Africa. His exact open-ocean track is unknown. Off southeastern Africa the Agulhas Current flows southwest and steep seas form when wind opposes it. In the Arabian Sea the summer south-west monsoon (roughly June–September) favours passages towards India and the winter north-east monsoon the reverse. Pilots there knew these sailing seasons long before 1490. The subtropical gyres circulate clockwise in the north and anticlockwise in the south. The later trans-Pacific return from the Philippines likewise sought westerlies farther north.
- Pitfalls:
  - Sailing straight from Spain to the west at 40° N as though the prevailing westerlies there favoured the outward passage
  - Hugging the African coast south of Guinea; coastal calms, the north-flowing Benguela Current and south-east trades can hinder progress
  - Treating the winds as seasonal luck; prevailing winds describe averages, the convergence zone migrates and storms can interrupt a favourable passage
  - Explaining the trade winds as 'the Earth spinning under the air'; the driver is hot air rising at the equator (Hadley 1735), turned by the Earth's rotation
  - Assuming a return route exists across the Pacific along the outbound latitude; the Spaniards lost ships for forty years before the eastward crossings of 1565
- History: india: by the 1st c. BC – Indian, Arab and Greek ships cross the Arabian Sea with the monsoon (the 1st-c. AD Periplus of the Erythraean Sea records the seasonal route); islamic: c. 1490 – Ibn Majid's Kitab al-Fawa'id gives monsoon sailing seasons for the whole Indian Ocean; china: 1405–1433 – Zheng He's fleets leave Fujian in winter with the north-east monsoon and return with the south-west; europe: 1430s–1440s – Portuguese volta do mar via the Azores; 1492–93 Columbus's outbound and return routes; 1497 da Gama's wide South Atlantic arc; 1513 Alaminos notes the Gulf Stream; 1565 Arellano and Urdaneta reach New Spain independently; Urdaneta's documented crossing helps establish the Manila–Acapulco route; 1686 Halley's trade-wind map; 1735 Hadley's explanation; 1770 Franklin–Folger Gulf Stream chart; global: Pacific – Polynesian navigators sail east against the trades, often in westerly spells, so they can run home if they find nothing
- Read:
  - Edmond Halley, An Historical Account of the Trade Winds, and Monsoons, Observable in the Seas between and near the Tropicks, Philosophical Transactions 16 (1686)
  - Alfred W. Crosby, Ecological Imperialism: The Biological Expansion of Europe, 900–1900 (1986)
  - J. H. Parry, The Discovery of the Sea (1974)
